summary:
Astro Health is an interactive research prototype that helps astronauts understand changes in their health during space missions. It brings five simulated health indicators, personal baselines, anomaly alerts, daily wellbeing check-ins, and follow-up notes into one dashboard.

The application establishes a seven-day baseline, highlights unusual readings, explains changes in plain language, and exports a mission report. Bundled biomarker summaries attributed to NASA’s OSD-575 and OSD-656 Inspiration4 studies inform simulation variability.

Astro Health addresses the challenge by connecting health-data gathering, interpretation, and follow-up in a clear visual workflow. Its intended benefit is to make complex information easier to understand while keeping physical indicators and personal context together. It demonstrates a foundation for future sensor integration and expert evaluation; it is not a clinically validated medical system.
details:
Astro Health explores how astronauts could gather health information, understand changes, and document follow-up through one accessible interface.

HOW IT WORKS

The application simulates five indicators: resting heart rate, sleep duration, bone mineral density, cumulative radiation exposure, and an experimental immune dysregulation index. The first seven simulated days establish a personal baseline. Trend screening and Isolation Forest anomaly detection help identify unusual patterns as the mission progresses.

Interactive charts show readings alongside their expected trends. When an indicator is flagged, the user can open a plain-language explanation, record a follow-up note, and update the alert’s review status. Reviewing an alert records an action; it does not establish medical clearance.

Daily check-ins add mood, energy, stress, sleep quality, and optional notes. An exportable JSON mission report combines readings, alerts, check-ins, follow-up, and data provenance.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project connects measurements with context and a documented next step. Its intended benefit is to help users notice changes and preserve useful information for later review. These benefits remain design goals rather than demonstrated clinical outcomes.

The creative element is the combination of personal-baseline monitoring, physical indicators, self-reported wellbeing, explanations, and follow-up in one workflow.

NASA DATA AND SCIENTIFIC SCOPE

Bundled biomarker summaries attributed to NASA OSDR studies OSD-575 and OSD-656 inform heuristic noise profiles for selected simulated indicators. NASA human-spaceflight resources and published research provide background for the modeled hazards.

The displayed telemetry is synthetic. The repository does not include a complete reproducible pipeline from the original study files to every bundled summary. Inspiration4’s four-person, three-day mission cannot validate long-duration forecasts, clinical alert thresholds, or the experimental immune index.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

The interface uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and Lucide icons. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, scikit-learn, and SQLite.

Explanations use local rules by default. An optional OpenRouter integration can provide model-generated explanations when explicitly enabled and configured. The recorded demonstration uses local explanations. No physical sensors are connected.

DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

The design emphasizes readable charts, clear status labels, transparent simulation limits, and local storage of check-ins and follow-up notes. Future work includes reproducible source-data processing, timestamped sensor inputs, missing-data checks, and evaluation of false alarms and usability with qualified experts.

TEAM AND DEVELOPMENT HISTORY

BoredtoMARS is a solo project by Ali Rayyan, participating in the Universal Event. ChatGPT/Codex and Claude assisted with development and project materials. Development began before the November 2026 hackathon.
